strengths: Well-motivated problem: Clearly identifies that ranking is easier than full CATE estimation, filling a genuine gap in the literature
Rigorous theory: Theorems 5.1 and 5.2 correctly establish Neyman-orthogonality and correct population minimizers using influence function methods; complete proofs in appendix are verifiable

Elegant technical construction: The progression from binary to soft to orthogonal ranking loss, with carefully designed pseudo-labels (Eq. 12) combining soft targets and doubly robust corrections, is well-motivated
Model-agnostic approach: Can instantiate with arbitrary ML models, providing flexibility not available in model-specific baselines like tree ranker

Comprehensive experiments: Multiple benchmarks (synthetic, 3 semi-synthetic domains), sensitivity analyses (overlap, pair subsampling), consistent improvements especially at small samples where theory predicts benefit (n=100: 0.94±0.21 vs 0.69±0.32 for plug-in ranker)
Excellent presentation: Clear motivation, well-structured progression, informative figures, detailed appendices supporting reproducibility
Fair experimental design: Sample splitting, consistent model architectures, multiple evaluation metrics (AUTOC, policy value), appropriate baseline comparisons
weaknesses: Hyperparameter complexity: κ requires validation-based model selection via approximated AUTOC, adding tuning burden with limited practical guidance and no empirical analysis of robustness to κ selection

Finite-sample stability concerns: Label clipping needed for pseudo-labels falling outside (0,1) in rare cases contradicts asymptotic orthogonality guarantees; no analysis of frequency or conditions triggering this
Missing finite-sample theory: No convergence rates or sample complexity analysis; gap between asymptotic orthogonality and practical behavior unexplored

Diminishing improvements at scale: At n=2,000 (Table 3), improvements over plug-in ranker negligible (1.37±0.00 vs 1.36±0.00); similar pattern in semi-synthetic results limits practical impact for well-resourced studies

Unexplained baseline comparison: Tree ranker outperforms Rank-Learner at smallest sample size (n=100: 1.01±0.16 vs 0.94±0.21) despite orthogonalization theoretically mattering most here; insufficient discussion of this result
Limited scope: Binary treatment only; no discussion of extension to continuous or multi-valued treatments; only synthetic/semi-synthetic experiments without real-world application
Incomplete analysis: No computational complexity breakdown despite O(n²) pair generation; training time comparisons absent; approximation error of AUTOC criterion not characterized
Presentation density: Notation heavy with multiple tildes and hats; interaction between κ in Eq. (10) vs (1/κ) in Eq. (13) subtle but not clearly explained upfront

strengths: Novel theoretical contribution: First Neyman-orthogonal two-stage learner for direct treatment effect ranking, filling a clear gap (Table 1)
Rigorous theory: Theorems 5.1 and 5.2 correctly establish orthogonality and identification via influence function analysis; proofs appear sound
Elegant loss construction: Orthogonal correction expressed as product of uncertainty weight and doubly robust score difference (Eq. 12-15)
Comprehensive experimental validation: Synthetic + 3 semi-synthetic datasets with proper methodology (sample splitting, cross-validation, 5 seeds)
Consistent empirical improvements especially in small-sample regimes where nuisance estimation error dominates (Tables 3-4)
Practical design: Model-agnostic framework with effective pair subsampling strategy; pair saturation at ~1% of n² pairs (Figure 3)
Strong reproducibility: Detailed DGPs, implementation details, hyperparameters; code promised; public semi-synthetic datasets
Clear presentation: Well-motivated problem with practical applications; logical progression from motivation to theory to experiments; Table 2 summary is effective
weaknesses: Modest practical improvements in large-sample regimes: At n=2000, Rank-Learner (1.37±0.00) vs DR-learner (1.36±0.02) with overlapping intervals; differences of 0.01-0.02 AUTOC in semi-synthetic settings
Tree ranker baseline (Kamran et al. 2024) actually outperforms Rank-Learner at n=100 (Table 7); limited analysis of why orthogonal advantage vanishes at smallest sample size
Stylized experimental settings: Synthetic DGP with obvious ranking structure; treatment effects generated from latent score; limited evaluation on realistic observational data
Theoretical gaps: No convergence rates provided for ||ĝ - g*||; label clipping for stability (Appendix E.3) could violate orthogonality but is not theoretically justified; no analysis of tie-breaking
κ selection under-explored: AUTOC approximation introduces hyperparameter; no sensitivity analysis on κ selection strategy; main text insufficiently emphasizes κ's importance
Lack of practitioner guidance: Paper doesn't clearly delineate which regimes favor Rank-Learner; no diagnostic tool to help practitioners choose between methods

Limited scope of comparisons: No empirical comparison to Vanderschueren et al. (2024) strategy beyond proxy with plug-in ranker; no comparison to robustness-to-confounding methods (e.g., Hess et al. 2026)
High-dimensional and computational aspects unexplored: All experiments d≤10; no runtime comparisons to baselines; no guidance on pair subsampling fraction selection
Stability implementation: Label clipping to (0,1) is post-hoc and could affect theory; paper doesn't discuss how frequently this occurs or propose principled alternatives

strengths: Clear problem formulation with compelling motivating examples (healthcare, marketing, policy); well-articulated insight that ranking is easier than CATE estimation
Sound theoretical contributions: Theorems 5.1 and 5.2 rigorously establish Neyman-orthogonality and characterize population minimizers; detailed proofs in appendices
Elegant methodological approach: smooth surrogate targets enabling orthogonalization; pseudo-label construction naturally incorporates doubly robust scores
Comprehensive experimental evaluation: synthetic, semi-synthetic, and real-world benchmarks across diverse domains; consistent empirical improvements with thorough ablation studies
Practical scalability insights: demonstrates ~1% of pairwise training samples sufficient for strong performance, addressing computational concerns
Model-agnostic framework: flexibility to use arbitrary ML models makes method accessible to practitioners
weaknesses: Limited theoretical novelty: core orthogonal loss construction technique from Kennedy (2024) and Chernozhukov et al. (2018); main contribution is applying existing methods to ranking setting
Critical gap in convergence analysis: no formal sample complexity, convergence rates, or asymptotic normality results despite claiming robustness guarantees; DR-learner and R-learner have such theory

Smoothness parameter κ design lacks rigor: introduced primarily for differentiability; selection via AUTOC validation requires estimating τ(x), somewhat contradicting the method's motivation; theoretical relationship to bias-variance tradeoff underdeveloped

Label clipping deviation from theory: pseudo-labels clipped to [0,1] for stability; Figure 7 shows empirical robustness but orthogonality guarantees are not theoretically characterized; unclear how much clipping compromises guarantees
No-ties assumption unrealistic: paper assumes τ(x) ties don't occur (page 4); robustness to near-ties where weight ω_τ amplifies noise not discussed; unrealistic for continuous covariates

Disconnect between population and finite-sample theory: Theorems 5.1–5.2 show L_orth and L_soft have identical population minimizers; orthogonality benefit appears only in finite samples but this is not rigorously characterized or formally analyzed
Limited real-world validation: only CRITEO uplift benchmark; AUUC is proxy metric without ground-truth τ; single dataset insufficient to demonstrate practical impact
Synthetic benchmarks use strictly increasing τ(X); real heterogeneity may be non-monotonic; generalization to complex effect structures unclear

Missing methodological details: validation set size sensitivity for AUTOC approximation not explored; quality of Chernozhukov et al. (2025) approximation not analyzed; computational cost (wall-clock time) comparisons with baselines absent

strengths: Well-motivated problem formulation distinguishing ranking from CATE estimation as fundamentally easier tasks
Rigorous theoretical development with Neyman-orthogonal learning objective proven in Theorems 5.1-5.2 and detailed influence function derivation in Appendix C
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across synthetic, semi-synthetic (3 datasets), and real-world benchmarks with consistent improvements over baselines
Practical considerations including computational scalability via pair subsampling, model-agnostic framework, and empirical orthogonality diagnostics
Thorough ablation studies on overlap sensitivity, κ selection, label clipping impact, and robustness to nuisance misspecification
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty—primarily combines existing elements (pairwise ranking, orthogonal learning via Kennedy 2024, doubly robust scores) rather than developing fundamentally new techniques
Significant gap between theory and practice: orthogonality proven but pseudo-labels are clipped in implementation (acknowledged in E.4), lacking theoretical analysis of impact
Absence of formal sample complexity analysis, convergence rates, or finite-sample bounds comparing ranking vs. CATE estimation despite this being core motivation
Smoothness parameter κ fundamentally changes problem formulation (scaled CATE at κ=1, pure ranking as κ→0) with no principled theoretical guidance for selection beyond empirical AUTOC
Modest empirical improvements in realistic settings—CRITEO results (Table 5, n=1M) show improvements near or within standard deviation ranges; fixed 1,000-sample test sets may lack statistical power
